'''Jack Cohen''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRSB}} (19 September 1933 – 6 May 2019)<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2019/jun/03/jack-cohen-obituary|title=Jack Cohen obituary|last=Stewart|first=Ian|date=2019-06-03|work=The Guardian|access-date=2019-06-06|language=en-GB|issn=0261-3077}}</ref> was a British [[Reproductive biology|reproductive biologist]] also known for his science books and involvement with science fiction.

==Life==
Cohen was born 19 September 1933 in [[Norwich]],<ref name=CV>{{cite web
 |url        = http://drjackcohen.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=62&Itemid=76
 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090526094808/http://drjackcohen.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=62&Itemid=76
 |url-status   = dead
 |archive-date = 26 May 2009
 |title      = Jack Cohen shorter CV
 |access-date = 10 October 2010
}}
</ref> but grew up in [[Stoke Newington]].<ref name=TJC>''The Jewish Chronicle'' 6 July 2005 "Not only connections"</ref> His father was killed shortly after the end of the [[World War II|Second World War]], 1 September 1945. His grandfather was a [[rabbi]] and Cohen was an observant [[Jew]] in his youth. He continued to attend the synagogue for cultural reasons. He was married three times and had six children.<ref name=TJC/>

==Academic career==
Cohen studied at [[University of Hull|University College, Hull]], where he obtained a BSc (external degree of the University of London) in 1954. He obtained his PhD in [[zoology]] at the same institution (by then [[Hull University]]) in 1957.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Cohen|first1=Jack|title=The inter-action between pigment cells and other feather germ components in the production of some colour patterns in feathers|url=http://blacklight.hull.ac.uk/catalogue/b1447133|website=University of Hull Library|publisher=University of Hull|access-date=18 September 2015|format=PhD thesis|date=1957}}{{Dead link|date=September 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>  He went to the [[University of Birmingham]] for post-doctoral work and was appointed lecturer in the Department of [[Zoology]] and [[Comparative physiology]] in 1959.  He worked for a year at [[Harvard Medical School]] then returned to [[University of Birmingham|Birmingham]] as a senior lecturer in 1968, a position he held until 1987. His former students include Sir [[Paul Nurse]], winner of the 2001 Nobel Prize for Medicine. In 1974 the [[University of Birmingham]] awarded him a [[DSc]] for his work.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Cohen|first1=Jack|title=Published Work in Developmental Biology|url=http://findit.bham.ac.uk/primo_library/libweb/action/dlDisplay.do?vid=44BIR_VU1&search_scope=default_scope&docId=44BIR_ALEPH_DS000047748&fn=permalink|website=University of Birmingham Library|publisher=University of Birmingham|access-date=18 September 2015|format=DSc thesis|date=1974}}</ref>

From 1987 to 1989 he was senior embryological advisor and manager of laboratories at the [[IVF]]/Infertility Clinic of a London private hospital.  From 1995 to 1996 he was visiting professor at the [[Weizmann Institute]], Israel. From 1996 to 2000 he was a consultant at the [[University of Warwick]], jointly to the Ecosystems Unit of the Biology Dept and the Mathematics Institute.   He was an honorary professor at the Mathematics Institute of the [[University of Warwick]]<ref name=UW>{{cite web |url=https://www2.warwick.ac.uk/fac/sci/maths/people/staff/jack_cohen |title=Professor Jack Cohen |website=University of Warwick |access-date=22 November 2017 }}</ref> and a visiting professor at [[Durham Business School]].

He published in prestigious journals such as [[Nature (journal)|''Nature'']] and wrote textbooks such as ''Living Embryos – an Introduction to the Study of Animal Development'' (1967) and ''Reproduction'' (1977). His theory of [[Sperm competition|sperm redundancy]]<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Cohen|first1=Jack|title=Correlation between Sperm "Redundancy" and Chiasma Frequency|journal=Nature|date=19 August 1967|volume=215|issue=5103|pages=862–863|doi=10.1038/215862a0|pmid=4964557|bibcode=1967Natur.215..862C|s2cid=45561203}}<!--|access-date=18 September 2015--></ref> was important in studies of fertility and treatment of infertility.

==Other activities==
Cohen worked as a consultant for [[science fiction television]] shows and science fiction novels regarding the creation of plausible [[extraterrestrial life|alien]]s. The writers who acknowledged his assistance included [[Anne McCaffrey]] for the ''[[Dragonriders of Pern]]''; [[Harry Harrison (writer)|Harry Harrison]] for his ''[[West of Eden|Eden]]'' trilogy; [[Larry Niven]], [[Jerry Pournelle]] and [[Steven Barnes]] for their ''[[The Legacy of Heorot|Legacy of Heorot]]''; [[James White (author)|James White]] of [[Sector General]] fame;<ref name="An interview with Dr. Jack Cohen">[http://library.thinkquest.org/C003763/index.php?page=interview05 An interview with Dr. Jack Cohen] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091007014039/http://library.thinkquest.org/C003763/index.php?page=interview05 |date=7 October 2009 }} Astrobiology: The Living Universe</ref> [[David Gerrold]] for the [[Chtorr]] ecology; and [[Terry Pratchett]] for several works.

Cohen and fellow [[University of Warwick]] researcher [[Ian Stewart (mathematician)|Ian Stewart]], a mathematician, collaborated with Terry Pratchett to write four ''[[Science of Discworld]]'' books, which accompany his ''Discworld'' series. Pratchett made them both "Honorary Wizards of the Unseen University" at the same 1999 ceremony where the University of Warwick gave Pratchett an honorary degree. Anne McCaffrey dedicated ''All the Weyrs of Pern'' (1991) to Jack and Judy Cohen and credited Jack with making fact of her fiction.

Cohen and Stewart also co-authored books on [[epistemology]].<!--Judging by the list of books below, someone who knows their work should be able to describe the Cohen & Stewart collaboration more effectively.-->

Cohen was a member of the high [[IQ]] society [[Mensa International|Mensa]].<ref name=Mensa>[https://secure.mensa.org.uk/download/1472/FAQs-_Apr-2008_2.pdf Mensa] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120223092634/https://secure.mensa.org.uk/download/1472/FAQs-_Apr-2008_2.pdf |date=23 February 2012 }} Frequently Asked Questions</ref> He was one of the small groups of British Mensans who persuaded science fiction author [[Isaac Asimov]] to visit the United Kingdom in June 1974.<ref>{{cite web|author=Andrew May |url=http://www.andrew-may.com/asf/asimov.htm |title=Isaac Asimov's First Visit to Britain |publisher=Andrew-may.com |access-date=7 June 2017}}</ref>

He had a long-standing interest in the design and natural balance of (particularly manmade) lake ecosystems, having designed new filtration systems but also led in reinstating Victorian designed systems at various locations around the UK (once describing Victorian ecosystems as failures of Frobenius integrability.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011arXiv1110.2154A/abstract |title=Comments about Hilbert's 16'th problem (final section by Jack Cohen) |access-date=13 May 2026}}</ref>)

In 2009, he became a [[patron]] of the anti-circumcision charity [[NORM-UK]].<ref>{{cite web
|url=http://www.norm-uk.org/news.html?action=showitem&item=1277
|title=NORM-UK welcomes Professor Jack Cohen
|publisher=NORM-UK
|date=14 September 2009
|access-date=14 September 2009
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100218114021/http://www.norm-uk.org/news.html?action=showitem&item=1277
|archive-date=18 February 2010
|url-status=dead
}}</ref>

His hobbies, according to the author profiles in his books, included [[boomerang]]-throwing and keeping strange animals. In fact, he kept a salt water aquarium and carefully nurtured a colony of amoebae for over 30 years, observations of which provided many useful ideas (Personal Communication with Jack Cohen, 2009. Communicated by William Sulis.)

==Books==
*''[[The Science of Discworld]]'', with [[Ian Stewart (mathematician)|Ian Stewart]] and [[Terry Pratchett]]
*''[[The Science of Discworld II: The Globe]]'', with [[Ian Stewart (mathematician)|Ian Stewart]] and [[Terry Pratchett]]
*''[[The Science of Discworld III: Darwin's Watch]]'', with [[Ian Stewart (mathematician)|Ian Stewart]] and [[Terry Pratchett]]
*''[[The Science of Discworld IV: Judgement Day]]'', with [[Ian Stewart (mathematician)|Ian Stewart]] and [[Terry Pratchett]]
*''[[Figments of Reality]]'', with [[Ian Stewart (mathematician)|Ian Stewart]] (non-fiction)
*''[[The Collapse of Chaos]]'', with [[Ian Stewart (mathematician)|Ian Stewart]] (non-fiction)
*''[[Evolving the Alien: The Science of Extraterrestrial Life]]'', with [[Ian Stewart (mathematician)|Ian Stewart]]. The American and second editions were published as ''What Does a Martian Look Like? The Science of Extraterrestrial Life''
*''[[Wheelers (novel)|Wheelers]]'', with [[Ian Stewart (mathematician)|Ian Stewart]] (fiction)
*''[[Heaven (2004 novel)|Heaven]]'' (fiction), with [[Ian Stewart (mathematician)|Ian Stewart]], {{ISBN|0-446-52983-4}}, Aspect (May 2004)
* ''Living Embryos'', Pergamon (1967)
* ''Reproduction'', Butterworths (1977)
* ''Spermatozoa, Antibodies and Infertility'' (1978) with W. F. Hendry
* ''Living Embryos'' (1981) with B. D. Massey
* ''Animal Reproduction: parents making parents'' (1984) with B. D. Massey
* ''The Privileged Ape'' (1989)
* ''Stop Working and Start Thinking'' (2000) with Graham Medley
